article_title: NSMQ Riddles: A Benchmark of Scientific and Mathematical Riddles for Quizzing Large Language Models
citation: George Boateng, Naafi Dasana Ibrahim, Samuel John, Philemon Badu, Patrick Agyeman-Budu, Jonathan Abrefah Mensah, Kevin Takyi Yeboah, William Edor, Andrew Kojo Mensah-Onumah, Nana Sam Yeboah, and Victor Kumbol. (2026). NSMQ Riddles: A Benchmark of Scientific and Mathematical Riddles for Quizzing Large Language Models. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07051
title: NSMQ Riddles: a benchmark of 1,840 scientific and mathematical riddles from Ghana's NSMQ competition
description: NSMQ Riddles is a benchmark dataset of scientific and mathematical riddles drawn from round 5 of Ghana's National Science and Maths Quiz, an annual live TV competition for senior secondary school students. The article states the dataset "consists of 1,840 riddle questions comprising 11 years of questions from round 5 of the NSMQ, ranging from 2009 to 2021". Each riddle contains a minimum of three clues that start vague and become more specific, with answers that are usually a number, word, or short phrase, allowing automatic evaluation via Exact Match and Fuzzy Match accuracy. It was curated from YouTube recordings and PDFs converted with OCR, manually reviewed, and preprocessed into CSVs with answer variants. A metadata sheet for 2019 and 2020 records which school answered each riddle and at which clue.
requirements: Access to the dataset for benchmarking requires emailing the authors, and automatic evaluation depends on the manually created ground-truth answer variants
constraints: Resource constraints allowed complete metadata curation for only 2019 and 2020; four riddles in 2019 have incomplete data due to video recording glitches; questions are publicly on YouTube so data contamination is possible but was not assessed
target_learners: senior secondary school students in Ghana
target_learning_goals: high-school level biology, chemistry, physics, and mathematics aligned with the WASSCE curriculum
examples: The authors parsed competition PDFs with Mathpix OCR, manually corrected transcription errors, and created answer variants such as SO2 and Sulphur (IV) Oxide to enable automatic evaluation
key_sources: George Boateng, Naafi Dasana Ibrahim, Samuel John, Philemon Badu, Patrick Agyeman-Budu, Jonathan Abrefah Mensah, Kevin Takyi Yeboah, William Edor, Andrew Kojo Mensah-Onumah, Nana Sam Yeboah, and Victor Kumbol. (2026). NSMQ Riddles: A Benchmark of Scientific and Mathematical Riddles for Quizzing Large Language Models. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07051

article_title: Snapshot Report – First-Year Persistence and Retention
citation: First-Year Persistence and Retention. (2017). National Student Clearinghouse Snapshot Report. https://nscresearchcenter.org/wp-content/uploads/NSC_SnapshotReport28_PersistenceRetention_Data_Tables.xlsx
title: National Student Clearinghouse first-year persistence and retention snapshot report and downloadable data tables
description: A National Student Clearinghouse snapshot report series tracking first-year persistence (continued enrollment at any institution) and retention (continued enrollment at the starting institution) for fall entering cohorts, with data current through fall 2016. The report defines its measures and cohort-selection rules and states that "Data tables for this snapshot may be downloaded from the NSC Research Center website" as an Excel file. It is sponsored in part by the Lumina Foundation.
requirements: Requires Clearinghouse enrollment and degree records covering participating institutions, with first-time status confirmed from historical records showing no prior college enrollment in the four years prior to the cohort year
constraints: Race and ethnicity data coverage is incomplete (79 percent of the fall 2015 cohort overall; 46 percent in the four-year for-profit sector, for which disaggregated results were omitted)

Beginning with fall 2015, non-degree-seeking students are reported separately, which the report says caused the 2015 spike in part-time retention rate; international students are now included and prior years restated
target_learners: first-time college students in U.S. higher education
target_learning_goals: institutional measurement of first-year student persistence and retention
examples: The report disaggregates fall 2015 rates by enrollment intensity, race and ethnicity, age at entry, and institutional sector, with trend figures covering 2009-2015 cohorts
key_sources: First-Year Persistence and Retention. (2017). National Student Clearinghouse Snapshot Report. https://nscresearchcenter.org/wp-content/uploads/NSC_SnapshotReport28_PersistenceRetention_Data_Tables.xlsx

citation: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2
title: NSF-funded longitudinal study of elementary and middle school math learning among ethnic minority students
description: Shell's tribute describes a research thread few in the field knew about: an NSF-funded in-depth longitudinal study of elementary and middle school student math learning and the factors influencing that learning, with a focus on understanding achievement of ethnic minority students, especially Native Americans. He reports that those involved "were actively engaged in manuscript writing right up to her passing," and hopes that as results are published the work will advance theory and practice in learning and motivation in the classroom.
requirements: The study was funded by the National Science Foundation and designed as an in-depth longitudinal study of math learning factors
constraints: At the time of the editorial the study's manuscripts were still being written and its results had not yet been published
target_learners: elementary and middle school students, especially ethnic minority students including Native Americans
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement and the factors influencing math learning
examples: The editorial reports collaborators were writing manuscripts from the study up to Moreno's passing, with results forthcoming
key_sources: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2

article_title: Supplemental Material for Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests
citation: Kennett, R., Martin, A. J., Pearson, J., Burns, E. C., & Collie, R. (2025). Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000964.supp
title: Teacher-designed standardized science achievement test aligned to NSW Stage 4 and 5 syllabuses
description: The science achievement test was built from NSW Stage 4 and 5 syllabus units, administered in two halves around an online science survey. Questions were developed by a lead science teacher with 26 years of experience, reviewed by a panel of five science educators for difficulty and syllabus alignment, with an additional review for linguistic accessibility for students from non-English speaking backgrounds. Items were coded dichotomously and scores standardized by year level.
requirements: An iterative review panel ensured content, format, structure, and accessibility met the panel's satisfaction, including a spread of difficulty levels typical of science assessments
constraints: The test measured selected content outcomes aligned with the NSW Stage 4 and Stage 5 science curriculum only
target_learners: high school science students, including students from non-English speaking backgrounds
target_learning_goals: measuring science achievement as the study's primary outcome
examples: A sample unit with introductory information supported by visual aids was presented to students using Qualtrics
key_sources: Kennett, R., Martin, A. J., Pearson, J., Burns, E. C., & Collie, R. (2025). Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests. article_title: An Examination of the Promise of the NumberShire Level 1 Gaming Intervention for Improving Student Mathematics Outcomes
citation: Hank Fien, Christian T. Doabler, Nancy J. Nelson, Derek B. Kosty, Ben Clarke & Scott K. Baker (2016). An Examination of the Promise of the NumberShire Level 1 Gaming Intervention for Improving Student Mathematics Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1119229
title: Differentiated Learning Pathway (DLP) for individualized routing within NS1
description: The DLP is NS1's mechanism for individualizing and intensifying instruction, calibrating activities to student skill levels using latency and accuracy metrics from game activities, with within- and between-activity adjustments that reroute students. "If the player scores less than 75% accuracy, she is routed to the additional instruction and guided practice pathway , a more intensive, individualized experience that provides reteaching and practice with the target skill." Scores of 75–89% route to additional practice on a prerequisite skill; 90% or greater continues the default pathway.
requirements: Performance metrics of latency and accuracy gathered during gameplay to calibrate instruction
Defined accuracy thresholds (90%, 75–89%, below 75%) that trigger routing decisions
target_learners: first-grade students struggling to master mathematics content
target_learning_goals: procedural skills and conceptual knowledge in whole-number mathematics
examples: A player scoring 75–89% on an independent practice activity is routed to additional practice on a previously mastered prerequisite skill
key_sources: Hank Fien, Christian T. Doabler, Nancy J. Nelson, Derek B. Kosty, Ben Clarke & Scott K. Baker (2016). An Examination of the Promise of the NumberShire Level 1 Gaming Intervention for Improving Student Mathematics Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1119229

article_title: Perceived vs. experienced care: a comparison between nursing students' self-assessed competence and patients' reported care.
citation: Ulupınar Fadime, Karasu Şeyda. (2025). Perceived vs. experienced care: a comparison between nursing students’ self-assessed competence and patients’ reported care. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-025-12880-w
title: Matched student–patient dyad instruments: NSCS and PPNSCS used to compare perceived competence and received care
description: The study pairs two validated instruments administered to matched student–patient dyads: the 43-item Nursing Students' Competence Scale with six subscales (total Cronbach's alpha 0.978) and the 28-item Patients' Perceptions of Nursing Students' Care Scale with four subscales, "scored on a 5-point Likert scale". The Turkish PPNSCS adaptation showed "good fit [RMSEA = 0.03, CFI = 0.99, Cronbach's alpha = 0.94]". Patients qualified only after at least eight hours of direct care from a participating student.
requirements: Patients must have received a minimum of eight hours of direct care from a participating student to form informed perceptions; students must be enrolled in clinical practice courses beyond first year.
constraints: Perceptions are self-reported and subjective; the cross-sectional design captures one point in time in a single hospital and healthcare system.
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students in clinical placements (years 2–4)
examples: Instruments were administered face-to-face in hospital wards between October 2024 and January 2025, each requiring approximately 10 minutes.
key_sources: Ulupınar Fadime, Karasu Şeyda. (2025). Perceived vs. experienced care: a comparison between nursing students’ self-assessed competence and patients’ reported care. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-025-12880-w

article_title: Effect of nursing simulation teaching information system based on HIS in comprehensive training course for senior nursing undergraduates: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Chen Yingshi, Feng Rixuan, Liu Mina, Yang Yang, Liu Huan, Zheng Wei, Zhao Yang, Luo Chenling. (2025). Effect of nursing simulation teaching information system based on HIS in comprehensive training course for senior nursing undergraduates: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07015-y
title: Nursing Simulation Teaching Information System (NSTIS)
description: The NSTIS is an academic hospital-information-system simulator developed by the research team since 2018, built on enterprise cloud management with a user layer, system management, teaching platform, and nurse workstation modules. Its nurse station "aligns with the HIS system configuration, enabling all HIS-related operations within the scope of the nurse's duties, such as medication administration, nursing assessments, and nursing documentation." Complete medical records follow simulation time in real time, cases can be duplicated per student, and a teaching auxiliary module supports scheduling, task release, homework upload, and self- and peer assessment. It was granted two patents in China.
requirements: Each bed in the nursing laboratory was equipped with a mobile nurse workstation and bedside information display to integrate the system into case simulations
Teachers received standardized training in system guidance and case simulation teaching
constraints: Nursing students' proficiency in operating the NSTIS remained insufficient even after training, which the authors say may have limited its effectiveness during simulation
Existing comparable systems focus mainly on recording nursing procedures and rarely divide cases into distinct clinical phases
target_learners: Third-year undergraduate nursing students in a comprehensive training course
target_learning_goals: HIS-related operations such as medical order processing and nursing documentation
Case simulation skills including assessment, health education, and nursing procedures
examples: In the trial, the experimental group used the NSTIS to obtain complete medical records and manage orders through system modules, while the control group used Microsoft Word case summaries and printed assessment sheets and orders
key_sources: Chen Yingshi, Feng Rixuan, Liu Mina, Yang Yang, Liu Huan, Zheng Wei, Zhao Yang, Luo Chenling. (2025). Effect of nursing simulation teaching information system based on HIS in comprehensive training course for senior nursing undergraduates: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07015-y
